title: The Drone
subtitle: A police drone films a peaceful procession; by noon the footage is being used to identify marchers
coldOpen: 10:00. A drone hovers over the students’ march.
The registrar is asked to confirm names.

briefing.grievance: Students marched peacefully for hostel fees. A police drone filmed every face. Now a list of names is circulating and the registrar has been asked to confirm them for “preventive action”.
knownFacts: The march had permission and ended without incident.
The drone was flown by the district police with no written order.
A list of forty names with photos is circulating on messaging apps.
unverifiedClaims: The list says the marchers were “paid by an outside group”.
A post says the drone footage shows students carrying weapons.
briefing.responsibility: You run the district administration. The registrar reports to you; so does the officer who flew the drone.
briefing.objective: Stop the misuse of the footage, protect the marchers from reprisal, and set a rule for surveillance of lawful assembly.

rightsMoments.question: Police filmed a lawful march to capture faces without a written order. What do privacy and assembly rights require?

options.text: Surveillance of lawful assembly needs a legal basis, a specific purpose and proportionality; footage must be preserved intact and face data deleted when no offence is alleged.
options.feedback: Correct. Privacy is a fundamental right; blanket face capture of a peaceful march fails legality, necessity and proportionality.

options.text: Police may film anyone in public and keep the faces indefinitely.
options.feedback: Public presence does not surrender privacy; targeted capture and retention need a lawful basis.

options.text: Delete all the footage immediately, including the parts that clear the marchers.
options.feedback: Exculpatory footage must be preserved; it is the identification data, not the record of peace, that must go.

rightsMoments.principle: Privacy (Puttaswamy, Article 21) and peaceful assembly (Article 19(1)(b)) mean surveillance needs law, purpose and proportion; face data from a lawful march must be deleted while the record is preserved.
rightsMoments.why: A sealed card and a deletion order protected both the truth and the marchers; a trimmed card would have lost both.

source.label: Constitution of India, Articles 21 and 22 (India Code)

simple.question: Police filmed a lawful march to capture faces, with no written order. What do privacy and assembly rights require?

options.a: Filming needs a law, a reason and limits. Keep the footage intact, delete the face data.
options.b: Police may film anyone outside and keep the faces forever.
options.c: Delete everything, including the parts that clear the marchers.

feedback.a: Yes! Privacy still applies in public. Keep the proof, delete the faces.
feedback.b: No. Being outside does not give up your privacy.
feedback.c: The footage that proves peace must be kept.

simple.principle: Filming a peaceful march needs a law, a reason and limits. Face data goes; the record stays.
simple.why: A sealed card and a deletion order protected the truth and the marchers.
